title: Electrochemistry
description: Cells, potentials, the Nernst equation, electrolysis, batteries and corrosion.
overview: Every battery, every fuel cell and every rusting bridge is a redox reaction whose two halves have been physically separated, so that the electrons must pass through a wire. If the reaction is spontaneous, the electrons do work. If it is not, a power supply can force it to run, which is how aluminum, chlorine and plated metals are made.

This chapter builds from the galvanic cell to cell potentials and their link to ΔG and K, introduces the Nernst equation for non-standard conditions, treats electrolysis quantitatively, and applies the ideas to batteries and corrosion.
objectives: Describe a galvanic cell and write its cell notation.
Calculate E°_cell from standard reduction potentials and predict spontaneity.
Use the Nernst equation to find the potential under non-standard conditions.
Use Faraday’s laws to relate charge to amount of substance in electrolysis.
Describe common batteries and how corrosion and its prevention work.

sections.title: Galvanic cells
body: A **galvanic** (voltaic) **cell** uses a spontaneous redox reaction to produce electric current. The oxidation and reduction half-reactions occur in separate **half-cells**, each an **electrode** in a solution of its ions, connected by an external wire and a salt bridge.

list: At the **anode**, oxidation occurs, and electrons are released. In a galvanic cell the anode is the negative terminal.
At the **cathode**, reduction occurs, and electrons are consumed. It is the positive terminal.

Electrons flow through the wire from anode to cathode. The **salt bridge** (a tube of inert electrolyte) completes the circuit by letting ions migrate, anions toward the anode and cations toward the cathode, so that neither half-cell builds up charge.

For a cell with no metal in a half-reaction (Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺, for example), an inert electrode of platinum or graphite carries the electrons.

check.q: In a galvanic cell, electrons flow…
check.a: From the anode to the cathode through the external wire
wrong: From the cathode to the anode through the wire
From the positive to the negative terminal

check.q: What does the salt bridge do?
check.a: Allows ions to migrate so each half-cell stays neutral

sections.title: Cell potentials and free energy
body: The **cell potential** E_cell, in volts (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹), measures the driving force of the reaction. It cannot be measured for a single half-cell, so each is compared with a reference, the **standard hydrogen electrode** (SHE): 2H⁺(aq, 1 M) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g, 1 bar), assigned E° = 0 V. Tables list **standard reduction potentials** E°, all written as reductions, under standard conditions (1 M, 1 bar, 25 °C).

head: Half-reaction
E° (V)
table.caption: Standard reduction potentials at 25 °C. The species at upper left are the strongest oxidizing agents, and those at lower right (the metals) the strongest reducing agents.

body: The more positive half-reaction runs as the reduction. A positive E°_cell means the reaction is spontaneous as written. **E° is an intensive property: do not multiply it by the stoichiometric coefficients.** This table also explains the activity series: metals low in the table (Zn, Mg) are oxidized by ions above them.

body: Moving n moles of electrons through a potential difference E does electrical work nFE, where F = 96,485 C mol⁻¹ is the **Faraday constant**. The maximum work equals −ΔG, so

eq: E° = (RT/nF) ln K = (0.05916 V / n) log K   at 25 °C

body: Positive E°, negative ΔG° and K > 1 all say the same thing.

check.a: The reaction is spontaneous as written

sections.title: The Nernst equation
body: Away from standard conditions, the free energy is ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. Substituting ΔG = −nFE gives the **Nernst equation**:

eq: E = E° − (0.05916 V / n) log Q   at 25 °C

body: As the cell discharges, Q rises toward K and E falls. At equilibrium E = 0: the battery is dead.

example.title: A non-standard cell
example.problem: What is the potential of the Zn–Cu cell with [Zn²⁺] = 1.0 M and [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 M?

body: A **concentration cell** has the same electrode material in both half-cells, with different concentrations. Its E° is zero, and the potential comes entirely from the Q term: electrons flow until the concentrations equalize. Nerve cells, which maintain a potential of about −70 mV across the membrane with K⁺ about 30 times more concentrated inside, behave like concentration cells. The glass **pH electrode** works on the same principle: E varies by 59 mV per pH unit.

example.title: A concentration cell
example.problem: Find the potential of Cu(s) | Cu²⁺(0.0010 M) || Cu²⁺(1.0 M) | Cu(s).
solution: The more dilute half-cell is the anode, where copper is oxidized to raise its concentration.

check.q: As a galvanic cell discharges, its potential…
check.a: Falls toward zero as Q approaches K

check.q: For a concentration cell, E° equals…
wrong: The potential of the more concentrated half-cell
The sum of both half-cell potentials

sections.title: Electrolysis
body: In **electrolysis** an external power source drives a nonspontaneous reaction in an **electrolytic cell**. The terminology stays the same: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode. The signs of the electrodes reverse, since the power source makes the anode positive and the cathode negative.

Electrolysis of molten NaCl gives sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode. In aqueous solutions water competes. In brine (the **chlor-alkali process**) the cathode produces H₂ and OH⁻ instead of sodium, and the anode produces Cl₂, for a net: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → Cl₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH. Aluminum is made by electrolysis of Al₂O₃ dissolved in molten cryolite near 960 °C (the **Hall–Héroult process**), consuming about 14 kWh per kilogram. In **electroplating**, the object to be coated is the cathode.
The amount of substance changed is proportional to the charge passed (**Faraday’s law**):

eq: n(substance) = Q / (z F)   (z = electrons per formula)

example.problem: How much copper is deposited by a current of 2.50 A passing for 1.00 h through CuSO₄ solution?

example.problem: How long does it take to deposit 5.00 g of silver from AgNO₃ at 0.500 A?

body.note: In practice a higher voltage than E° is needed, the overpotential, because of slow electrode kinetics. This is why water is not oxidized in preference to chloride in brine, though E° for O₂ is lower than for Cl₂.

sections.title: Batteries and fuel cells
body: A **battery** is one or more galvanic cells in series. A **primary** battery cannot be recharged (the cell reaction is consumed or irreversible). A **secondary**, or **rechargeable**, battery can be driven in reverse by an external voltage.

head: Type
Anode / cathode reaction
Voltage per cell
Notes
rows: Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻ / PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O
Rechargeable; six cells make a 12 V car battery
LiC₆ → C₆ + Li⁺ + e⁻ / Li₁₋ₓCoO₂ + xLi⁺ + xe⁻ → LiCoO₂
Rechargeable; Li⁺ shuttles between graphite and an oxide
table.caption: Common batteries.

body: The lead–acid reaction is Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. During discharge, sulfuric acid is consumed, so the density of the electrolyte shows the state of charge. A lithium-ion cell stores energy by moving lithium ions between layered electrodes without changing the electrode structure, which is why it can be recharged hundreds of times and has high energy density. A **fuel cell** is a galvanic cell fed continuously with fuel and oxidant, and it is not depleted as long as supplies continue.

check.a: Its cell reaction can be reversed by applying an external voltage
wrong: It is not a galvanic cell

sections.title: Corrosion
body: **Corrosion** is the oxidation of a metal by its environment. Rusting is an electrochemical process. Iron is oxidized at an anodic region of the surface, with electrons flowing through the metal to a cathodic region, where oxygen is reduced. The ions meet in the water film between them:

eq: Fe²⁺ is further oxidized to rust, Fe₂O₃·nH₂O

body: Both water and oxygen are required, and dissolved salt speeds the process by carrying current, which is why cars rust faster where roads are salted. Rust flakes off and exposes fresh metal. Aluminum also oxidizes, but its oxide forms a thin, tight layer that protects the metal beneath.

list: **Barriers**: paint, oil and plastic coatings keep out water and oxygen. They fail once scratched.

**Galvanizing** coats steel with zinc. Zinc (E° = −0.76 V) is oxidized in preference to iron (−0.44 V), so even where the coating is scratched, the steel remains protected: zinc is a **sacrificial anode**.

**Cathodic protection** attaches a block of a more active metal, such as magnesium, to a pipeline, ship hull or water heater. The block corrodes, and the structure becomes the cathode. Tin plating, by contrast, protects only while intact: tin (E° = −0.14 V) is less active than iron, so once the coating is scratched the iron corrodes faster.

check.a: Zinc is more easily oxidized than iron and corrodes instead
wrong: Zinc forms a covalent bond to iron

quiz.q: A galvanic cell oxidizes copper metal and reduces Ag⁺. Which cell notation is correct?
quiz.why: The anode (oxidation) is written on the left, with a double line for the salt bridge. Each half-cell lists the electrode phase and its ion separated by a single phase-boundary line.

quiz.q: In a Zn(s) | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu(s) cell, toward which side do anions of the salt bridge migrate, and why?
quiz.a: Toward the zinc half-cell, to balance the Zn²⁺ being produced
wrong: Toward the copper half-cell, to replace the Cu²⁺ being consumed
Toward both half-cells equally, so that no net charge moves
Anions do not move; only electrons cross between the half-cells
quiz.why: Oxidation at the anode adds positive charge to its solution, and anions move toward the anode to cancel it. Cations move toward the cathode, where Cu²⁺ is being used up.

quiz.q: A half-cell contains only Fe³⁺ and Fe²⁺ in solution. What electrode is used?
quiz.a: An inert one, such as platinum or graphite
wrong: An iron rod, since iron appears in the half-reaction
None, since the solution conducts electrons
A copper rod, since it is a good conductor
quiz.why: No solid metal takes part in Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺, so an unreactive conductor is needed to deliver or receive electrons. Iron would itself react.

quiz.q: What is E°_cell for the reaction Fe(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s)?
quiz.why: E° = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.80 − (−0.44) = +1.24 V. The coefficient 2 on Ag⁺ does not change it, and doubling 0.80 gives the wrong +2.04 V.

quiz.q: Which reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions?
quiz.why: Only the first has a positive E°: 0.34 − (−0.44) = +0.78 V. In each other reaction the metal being oxidized has the higher (more positive) reduction potential.

quiz.q: A cell reaction has E° = +0.118 V with n = 2 at 25 °C. What is K?
quiz.why: log K = nE°/0.05916 = 2(0.118)/0.05916 = 4.0, so K = 1 × 10⁴. Omitting n gives 1 × 10², and a positive E° always gives K > 1.

quiz.q: A balanced cell equation is multiplied by 2. What happens to E°_cell and ΔG°?
quiz.a: E° is unchanged and ΔG° doubles
wrong: E° doubles and ΔG° is unchanged
quiz.why: E° is intensive, a driving force per unit charge, so it does not scale. ΔG° = −nFE° is extensive, and n doubles with the equation.

quiz.q: What is E for the Zn–Cu cell (E° = 1.10 V, n = 2) when [Zn²⁺] = 0.010 M and [Cu²⁺] = 1.0 M?
quiz.why: Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 0.010, so E = 1.10 − (0.05916/2)(−2) = 1.16 V. Low product concentration raises the potential. Leaving out the factor of 1/n gives 1.22 V.

quiz.q: A cell has Ag electrodes in 0.010 M Ag⁺ and in 0.10 M Ag⁺ at 25 °C. What is its potential, and which is the anode?
quiz.a: 0.059 V; the electrode in 0.010 M Ag⁺
wrong: 0.059 V; the electrode in 0.10 M Ag⁺
0.118 V; the electrode in 0.010 M Ag⁺
0 V, because both electrodes are silver
quiz.why: E° = 0, so E = −(0.05916/1) log(0.010/0.10) = +0.059 V. Oxidation at the dilute side raises its Ag⁺ concentration, so concentrations move toward equality.

quiz.q: A glass pH electrode changes potential by 59 mV per pH unit. By how much does its potential change if the pH goes from 7.0 to 4.0?
quiz.why: The potential is linear in pH, so 3 units correspond to 3 × 59 ≈ 177 mV. It is not proportional to the concentration, which changes by a factor of 1000.

quiz.q: A current of 3.00 A flows for 30.0 min through NiSO₄ solution. What mass of nickel plates onto the cathode? (M = 58.69 g mol⁻¹)
quiz.why: Q = 3.00 × 1800 s = 5400 C, which is 0.0560 mol of e⁻. Ni²⁺ needs two electrons, so 0.0280 mol Ni = 1.64 g. Forgetting to convert minutes to seconds (90 C) gives 0.0274 g.

quiz.q: How long must 10.0 A pass through brine to make 0.100 mol of Cl₂ at the anode?
quiz.why: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ takes 0.200 mol e⁻, which is 19,300 C. At 10.0 A, t = 1930 s. Using one electron per Cl₂ gives half of this.

quiz.q: A concentrated aqueous NaCl solution is electrolyzed. What forms at each electrode?
quiz.a: H₂ and OH⁻ at the cathode; Cl₂ at the anode
wrong: Na at the cathode; Cl₂ at the anode
H₂ at the cathode; O₂ at the anode
Na at the cathode; O₂ at the anode
quiz.why: Water is reduced more easily than Na⁺. At the anode O₂ evolution would be favored by E°, but its overpotential is high, so Cl⁻ is oxidized instead.

quiz.q: In an electrolytic cell, the anode is
quiz.a: the positive electrode, and oxidation occurs there
wrong: the negative electrode, and oxidation occurs there
the positive electrode, and reduction occurs there
the negative electrode, and reduction occurs there
quiz.why: Oxidation always occurs at the anode. The external supply pulls electrons away from it, making it positive, which is the reverse of the sign in a galvanic cell.

quiz.q: The electrolyte density of a lead–acid battery falls during discharge because
quiz.a: H₂SO₄ is consumed as PbSO₄ and water form
wrong: water is consumed at the cathode
quiz.why: The overall discharge reaction is Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. Sulfate leaves solution as solid PbSO₄ and water is produced, so the density tracks the state of charge.

quiz.q: How does a hydrogen fuel cell differ from a primary battery?
quiz.a: Fuel and oxidant are supplied continuously, so it is not used up while they last
wrong: It does not involve a redox reaction
It is charged by driving the cell reaction in reverse
It has no anode or cathode
quiz.why: Both are galvanic cells with electrodes and redox reactions. A battery has its reactants built in, and a fuel cell gets them from outside.

quiz.q: The tin coating on a steel can is scratched, exposing the iron. Compared with the bare steel, the iron
quiz.a: corrodes faster, because tin is less easily oxidized than iron
wrong: is protected, because tin is more easily oxidized than iron
corrodes at the same rate as bare steel
is protected, because the tin still blocks oxygen
quiz.why: Tin (−0.14 V) is less active than iron (−0.44 V), so the iron becomes the anode of a small galvanic cell and is oxidized. Zinc (−0.76 V), by contrast, protects the iron.

quiz.q: Why do cars rust faster where roads are salted?
quiz.a: Dissolved ions carry current between the anodic and cathodic regions of the metal
wrong: Salt reacts directly with iron to form rust
Salt lowers the E° of the oxygen reduction
Salt supplies the oxygen needed for rusting
quiz.why: Rusting is a short-circuited galvanic cell, and ions in the water film complete the circuit. Salt is not a reactant: rust needs only iron, oxygen and water.

summary: A galvanic cell separates oxidation (anode, −) from reduction (cathode, +). Electrons flow through the wire and ions through the salt bridge.
E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode, with no scaling by coefficients. A positive E° means a spontaneous reaction.
ΔG° = −nFE°, and E° = (0.05916/n) log K at 25 °C.
Nernst: E = E° − (0.05916/n) log Q. A discharged battery has Q = K and E = 0.
Faraday’s law: n = It/(zF). One mole of electrons is 96,485 C.
Batteries are galvanic cells in series. Rusting is a galvanic process, prevented by barriers, zinc coatings and sacrificial anodes.

problems.q: Write the cell reaction and calculate E°, ΔG° and K for a cell made of Zn²⁺/Zn and Ag⁺/Ag half-cells.
problems.solution: Ag⁺ is the stronger oxidant: cathode Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag (×2); anode Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Overall Zn + 2Ag⁺ → Zn²⁺ + 2Ag. E° = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V, n = 2. ΔG° = −2(96,485)(1.56) = −301 kJ. log K = 2(1.56)/0.05916 = 52.7, K = 5 × 10⁵².
